title: FlowNar: Scalable Streaming Narration for Long-Form Videos
claim: Baselines' memory grows with input length until they fail and run slowly; ours stays bounded, scaling to far longer inputs at higher throughput.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right: example outputs, memory line plot, throughput bars; dashed 24GB limit
description: Three panels. The left panel shows three egocentric video frames with timestamps along a streaming-time arrow. Below, two rows of text captions compare Videollm-online and Ours. Videollm-online produces 'You get out of the van' and 'You enter the restaurant', then an red 'OOM!' burst. Ours, below a dashed divider, continues with 'You eat the pizza.' The middle panel is a log-x line plot of VRAM in GB against processed frames. Baseline curves, dashed for 8B, climb past a dashed 24 GB line, while Ours and Ours-C stay flat. A red arrow marks '10x longer'. The right panel is a grouped bar chart of FPS, with solid bars for 1B and hatched bars for 8B. Ours and Ours-C bars are highest, at 28.7 and 33.4. Colors are blue, purple, orange and green per method.
caption: Efficiency and scalability comparison of \ours, Videollm-online [ref], and Videollm-mod [ref]. (Left) Example streaming outputs: Videollm-online can encounter out of memory (OOM) errors while \ours continues. (Middle) VRAM usage vs.\ processed frames (log scale): memory usage for both baselines grows rapidly and exceeds a typical GPU limit (24GB, dashed line), whereas \ours variants remain compact, supporting 10$\times$ longer videos relative to Videollm-online. (Right) Throughput (FPS) on an H100 measured over 10K frames: \ours achieves roughly 3$\times$ higher FPS than Videollm-online.
abstract: Recent Large Multimodal Models (LMMs), primarily designed for offline settings, are ill-suited for the dynamic requirements of streaming video. While recent online adaptations improve real-time processing, they still face critical scalability challenges, with resource demands typically growing at least linearly with video duration. To overcome this bottleneck, we propose FlowNar, a novel framework for scalable streaming video narration. The core of FlowNar is a dynamic context management strategy for historical visual context removal, combined with our CLAM (Cross Linear Attentive Memory) module for streaming visual history retention, ensuring bounded visual memory usage and computational complexity, crucial for efficient streaming. We also introduce a realistic self-conditioned evaluation protocol and complementary evaluation metrics to assess streaming narration models under deployment-like conditions. Experiments on the Ego4D, EgoExo4D, and EpicKitchens100 datasets demonstrate that FlowNar substantially improves narration quality over strong baselines while being highly efficient, supporting processing of 10$\times$ longer videos and achieving 3$\times$ higher throughput (FPS). The code is available at https://github.com/zeyun-zhong/FlowNar.
